Ceva Cradle

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: Move the dots and watch two triangles of lines: when the three lines from the corners meet in one spot, the three lines inside also meet.
How to play: Drag A, B, C, O or X, Y, Z with a mouse or finger, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Tick "cevians" and "hint" to see the lines and the proof.
Look for the math

Take a triangle ABC, put X, Y and Z on its sides, and pick any other point O. Join O to the three corners. The lines AO, BO and CO cross the sides of the little triangle XYZ at D, E and F. Drag the dots: something stays exactly the same.

Two triangles, six lines

The three lines AX, BY and CZ belong to the big triangle. The three lines XD, YE and ZF belong to the small one. Tick "cevians" to see both sets. Tick "hint" to see the two perpendiculars YG and ZH dropped from Y and Z onto AO; they are the key to the proof on the original page.

The product that never changes

Measure the lengths along the sides and multiply three ratios for each triangle. The applet's page claims that the two answers are always the same:

(AZ/ZB)(BX/XC)(CY/YA) = (ZD/DY)(YF/FX)(XE/EZ)

The left side only knows where X, Y and Z sit. The right side uses D, E and F, which move with O — yet the two stay equal. The logic test checks this on more than 1,500 random diagrams and on 720 placements of O around fixed cradles; the largest relative difference it found was about 10-11. Move O far out of the picture and the equality still holds.

Why O cancels

From the similar right triangles at D, ZD/DY = ZH/YG. Then ZH = AZ·sin(OAZ) and YG = YA·sin(OAY), so ZD/DY = (AZ/YA)·sin(OAZ)/sin(OAY). Two analogous formulas give the other ratios. Multiplying all three leaves exactly the left-hand product above, times a product of six sines.

Those six sines cancel because AO, BO and CO already meet at O: that is the trigonometric form of Ceva's theorem. So the point O never enters the identity at all.

When the lines meet

Each product is 1 exactly when its three cevians pass through one point — the ordinary Ceva's theorem. Since the products are equal, the six lines meet together or not together: the cevians AX, BY, CZ concur if and only if XD, YE and ZF concur. The applet called a diagram finished when both products were within 0.01 of 1; this page uses the same test, and draws the two meeting points M and N in green and purple.

Try putting X, Y and Z at the midpoints of the sides: the first three lines meet at the centre. Now slide O anywhere — the second three lines still meet.
